hero.headline: Agents that hold under load.

steps.label: 01 — Your data
steps.headline: The first pier: data that never leaves.
steps.body: Retrieval runs next to your systems, not ours. Personal data is minimised before a model ever sees it, and every read is logged.

steps.label: 02 — Your models
steps.headline: The second pier: open-weight models on your hardware.
steps.body: We fit the model to the job and run it where you choose — your GPUs, your cloud account, or a hosted API when that is genuinely the better call.

steps.label: 03 — The keystone
steps.headline: Governance locks it together.
steps.body: Human-in-the-loop by default, autonomy earned in stages you control, and an evaluation harness that tells you when something drifts.

steps.label: 04 — In production
steps.headline: Five days to a prototype. Weeks to production.
steps.body: A running agent on your real data in five days, then exception paths, guardrails and handover. You own the code, the infrastructure and the docs.

items.text: You own the code, the infra and the docs from day one
Every engagement has one metric, agreed before we write code

problem.headline: Your team is the integration layer.
problem.body: Someone reads the WhatsApp message, opens the CRM, checks the ERP, types the reply, sets a reminder to follow up — and does it again four hundred times a month. That work is not hard. It is just relentless, and it is why your people are busy instead of useful.

points.title: Enquiries decay
points.body: A lead that waits four hours is a lead someone else already answered.

points.title: Follow-ups leak
points.body: The second and third chase are where the revenue is, and they are the first thing a busy team drops.

points.title: Systems don't talk
points.body: The CRM knows one thing, the ERP another, WhatsApp a third. A human reconciles them, badly, all day.

servicesIntro.headline: Four things. We do them properly.
servicesIntro.body: We keep the menu short on purpose. A four-item list we can execute beats a twenty-item list that makes us a generalist.

howItWorks.headline: Five days to something real. Four to six weeks to production.
howItWorks.body: The speed is not a stunt. It is the only advantage a small team genuinely has over a large one, so we built the whole process around protecting it.

steps.title: A call, then a memo
steps.body: A founder takes the call — no SDR, no deck. Afterwards you get a written build memo: what we would build, what it should move, what it takes, and what we would not build. Sometimes the memo says wait. We send it anyway.

steps.title: Access and the data audit
steps.body: We look at the data your agent will read before we promise anything about the agent. An agent is only as good as what it can see, and this is where most projects quietly fail.

steps.title: Working prototype
steps.body: Not a slide. A running agent on your real data, handling the real workflow, that you can break in front of us.

steps.title: Production, with guardrails
steps.body: Exception paths, audit trail, human-in-the-loop review queue, staged rollout from supervised to autonomous. The unglamorous half is the half that decides whether it survives.

steps.title: Keys, then a choice
steps.body: Code, infrastructure, prompts, evaluation harness and documentation are yours. Keep running it yourself, or put it on a managed plan. Both are real options — that is the point.

proof.headline: Every engagement publishes a number.
proof.body: We instrument the metric before we write code, because a project you cannot measure is a project you cannot sell twice.

assistantPitch.headline: Meet Sakha. It is running right now, on the right of your screen.

Ask it something hard.

items.name: Customer response agents
items.oneLiner: Answer every customer in under a minute, on the channel they already use.
items.body: An agent that reads incoming messages on WhatsApp, web chat, email or a phone line, understands what is actually being asked, looks the answer up in your systems, and replies. Not a decision-tree bot — it reads your live order data, your price list and your policies, and it hands over to a human the moment it is out of its depth.
outcomes: First response measured in seconds instead of hours
Out-of-hours and weekend cover with no rota
includes: WhatsApp Business API, web chat, email or voice
Retrieval over your real catalogue, policies and order data
Confidence thresholds with automatic human handover
items.goodFitWhen: You get more than roughly 200 repetitive enquiries a month and the answers already exist somewhere in your systems.
items.notAFitWhen: Your answers live only in one person's head and nowhere else. Fix that first — we will tell you how, and it does not need us.

items.name: Follow-up and revenue agents
items.oneLiner: The second and third chase, done every time, by something that never gets busy.
items.body: Most revenue leaks in the gap between interest and action. This agent watches your pipeline, chases quotes that went quiet, confirms and re-confirms appointments, recovers abandoned carts, and keeps your CRM honest without anyone typing into it.
outcomes: A CRM that reflects reality without manual data entry
Follow-up that happens on the third attempt, not just the first
includes: Escalation to a human when the reply is not routine
items.goodFitWhen: You have a defined pipeline and you know follow-up is being dropped.
items.notAFitWhen: You have no CRM at all. Start there — an agent cannot chase a pipeline that does not exist.

items.name: Internal operations agents
items.oneLiner: Give your own team the answer instead of the form.
items.body: An agent your staff talk to instead of raising a ticket. Leave balances, policy questions, order status, stock levels, approval routing, report generation. It reads your HR system, your ERP and your document store, and it can act — file the request, book the slot, raise the invoice — inside the permissions you give it.
outcomes: Tier-one internal tickets absorbed rather than queued
Managers stop being a lookup service
Policy answered consistently, with the source cited
includes: Read access across HR, ERP, finance and document stores
Scoped write actions with approval steps
Per-role permissions, so people see only what they should
Cited answers — every response links to the document behind it
items.goodFitWhen: The same twenty questions reach your managers every week.
items.notAFitWhen: Your policies contradict each other. The agent will surface that contradiction publicly, which is useful but rarely comfortable.

items.name: System integration and data groundwork
items.oneLiner: Your agent is only as good as the data it can read.
items.body: The least glamorous service and the one that decides whether the others work. We connect the systems that do not talk — CRM, ERP, accounting, spreadsheets, that one Windows machine in the back office — clean up what the agent will read, and build the connector layer once so every future agent inherits it.
outcomes: One connector layer that every later agent reuses
Data quality problems found before they become agent failures
No more manual re-keying between systems
includes: Data audit with a written findings report
Connectors for your CRM, ERP and accounting stack
Browser automation where a system has no API
items.goodFitWhen: Almost always. We usually recommend starting here.
items.notAFitWhen: Never, honestly — but it can sometimes be scoped smaller than you expect. We will tell you when.

reusableModules.headline: We do not rebuild the plumbing for every client.
reusableModules.body: Authentication, WhatsApp delivery, document search, CRM sync, payment capture, voice, analytics and the human-review queue are built once and configured per client. You pay for the part of your problem that is genuinely yours, not for us to write a login screen again.

hero.headline: Made possible by two friends, with trust and grit.
hero.subhead: That sentence is not marketing. It is the entire origin of the company, and it is still how decisions get made here.

story.headline: Why 'Asphalix'
body: Asphalēs is Greek for 'not liable to fall'. An arch holds because of its keystone: the harder you press, the tighter it locks. That is what we want our agents to be — systems that hold under load, not demos that fall over in month four.
We started as Sakha AI. Sakha means friend — in the older sense, someone who tells you the truth even when a more agreeable answer was available. The company outgrew the name; our assistant kept it.

We picked it because the thing we kept noticing about this industry is how much of it is agreeable. Every vendor says yes. Every pilot is a success right up until the point where nobody can say what it changed. Nobody publishes a failure, and the software quietly stops being used about four months after the case study goes out.

So we built the company around the three things we could actually promise on day one, with no funding and no logos: we would be fast, we would be honest about what not to build, and we would go deep in a few places instead of shallow everywhere.
Trust and grit were the only assets two friends had at the start. They turned out to be the right ones.

meta.description: The one-page checklist that goes into every Asphalix proposal.

hero.headline: The checklist that goes in every proposal.
hero.subhead: Enterprise buyers ask for this and most small firms have nothing to hand them. It costs us nothing to have written it down, and it wins the compliance-nervous buyer that scares other boutiques off.

autonomyLevels.name: Shadow
autonomyLevels.description: The agent drafts, a human sends. Nothing reaches a customer without review. Every engagement starts here.

autonomyLevels.name: Supervised
autonomyLevels.description: The agent acts on routine cases and routes anything below its confidence threshold to a human queue.

autonomyLevels.name: Autonomous with exceptions
autonomyLevels.description: The agent handles the defined workflow end to end. Named exception categories always escalate.

autonomyLevels.name: Autonomous
autonomyLevels.description: Full autonomy inside a scoped domain, with sampled human review and alerting on drift. Reached by evidence, never by default.

checklist.item: Named metric agreed and instrumented before build
checklist.why: An unmeasured agent cannot be defended or improved.

checklist.item: Data audit completed and findings shared in writing
checklist.why: Most agent failures are data failures wearing a costume.

checklist.item: Autonomy level agreed and written into the scope
checklist.why: So nobody discovers after launch that it was sending emails on its own.
Somewhere for the agent to put the things it should not decide.

checklist.item: Audit trail of every agent action, retained and queryable
checklist.why: When someone asks 'why did it do that', there is an answer.

checklist.item: Escalation and exception paths defined per workflow
checklist.why: The unhappy path is where trust is won or lost.

checklist.item: PII handling documented; identifiers minimised in model calls
checklist.why: Send the model what it needs, never the whole record.

checklist.item: Access scoped per role, least privilege by default
checklist.why: An agent should not see more than the person asking.
Ship to ten percent before you ship to everyone.

checklist.item: Evaluation harness handed over with the code
checklist.why: So you can prove in six months that it still works.
